era: Jesus to Chalcedon, c. AD 30 to 451

nodes.name: Jesus and apostles
nodes.summary: Jesus' followers proclaimed his resurrection, gathered in Jerusalem, and spread the gospel through Jewish and Gentile communities.
nodes.why: Every later Christian tradition traces its roots to Jesus and the apostles.
facts: Jesus' crucifixion and resurrection traditionally date around AD 30 or 33.
Jerusalem's first believers remained connected to Jewish worship.
Apostles taught, baptized, and celebrated the Lord's Supper.
nodes.sacraments: No fixed sacrament count. Baptism marks entry into Christ. The Lord's Supper shares in his body and blood. Both are central to worship.
nodes.today: Later Christian traditions claim this inheritance. No separate membership.
nodes.disputed: Traditions disagree about infant baptism, Eucharistic presence, and church authority in this period.

nodes.name: Pentecost
nodes.summary: Acts describes the Holy Spirit empowering Jesus' followers in Jerusalem. Peter preached, and about 3,000 people received baptism.
nodes.why: The church's first shared life joined the Holy Spirit's work with preaching, baptism, and worship.
facts: The traditional date is approximately AD 30 or 33.
Acts 2 connects baptism with repentance and forgiveness.
Believers shared teaching, prayer, meals, and possessions.

nodes.name: Paul's missions
nodes.summary: Paul and coworkers established Gentile churches across Asia Minor and Greece. His letters explained faith, church life, baptism, and the Lord's Supper.
nodes.why: Paul brought the gospel to Gentile communities. His letters still shape Christian teaching about baptism and the Lord's Supper.
facts: Paul traveled with Barnabas, Silas, Timothy, and others.
Acts describes three missionary journeys, followed by his journey to Rome.
His letters address real congregations and their conflicts.

nodes.name: Council of Jerusalem
nodes.summary: Apostles and elders decided Gentile converts did not need circumcision. Acts records shared food restrictions intended to support fellowship.
nodes.why: Gentiles could become Christians without circumcision. The council gave churches an early example of settling disputes together.
facts: The meeting probably occurred around AD 48 or 49.
Peter, James, Paul, and Barnabas appear in Acts 15.
The council rejected circumcision as a requirement for Gentile salvation.

nodes.name: Jerusalem falls
nodes.summary: Roman troops under Titus destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple during the Jewish revolt. The disaster transformed the setting of Jewish and Christian life.
nodes.why: Jerusalem's destruction ended Temple worship and weakened the city's role as Christianity spread elsewhere.
facts: Rome destroyed the Second Temple in AD 70.
Christian communities already existed beyond Judea.
Christianity's separation from Judaism developed gradually over many years.

nodes.name: Early church
nodes.summary: Churches developed bishops, shared Scriptures, creeds, and sacramental worship. They faced persecution and doctrinal disputes before the major fifth-century separations.
nodes.why: Catholics, Orthodox Christians, and many Protestants share beliefs and worship practices inherited from these churches.
facts: Local churches differed in customs and leadership arrangements.
Baptism and Eucharist remained central to Christian membership and worship.
Disputes over Ephesus and Chalcedon led to lasting divisions.
nodes.sacraments: No universally fixed count. Baptism gives cleansing and new birth. Eucharist shares Christ's body and blood. Practices develop, including infant baptism, confirmation, penance, and ordination.
nodes.today: Living Christian traditions inherit these churches. No separate membership.
nodes.disputed: An undivided church is a map simplification. Rival Christian groups and earlier local schisms already existed.

nodes.name: Roman persecutions
nodes.summary: Roman authorities sometimes punished Christians for refusing sacrifice or public worship. Persecution varied by emperor and region, ending broadly with toleration.
nodes.why: Persecution gave churches martyrs to remember and forced decisions about whether Christians who renounced their faith could return.
facts: Nero punished Christians in Rome in AD 64, before this branch begins.
Decius demanded sacrifices across the empire in AD 250.
Diocletian's persecution began in AD 303.
Galerius granted toleration in 311. Milan extended protections in 313.

nodes.name: Didache
nodes.summary: An early Christian handbook describes moral teaching, baptism, Eucharistic prayers, fasting, and local ministers. Its instructions reveal worship before later sacramental systems.
nodes.why: Early Christians baptized in the Trinity's name, allowed pouring when necessary, and reserved Communion for baptized believers.
facts: The text probably dates around the late first or early second century.
It prefers running water and allows threefold pouring when needed.
It limits Eucharistic participation to baptized believers.
Sunday gatherings include breaking bread and confessing sins.
nodes.disputed: Scholars debate its date and whether some meal prayers describe Eucharist, a fellowship meal, or both.

nodes.name: Ignatius of Antioch
nodes.summary: Ignatius wrote letters urging churches to unite around their bishop and confess Christ's real humanity. He described the Eucharist as Christ's flesh.
nodes.why: Ignatius linked unity under a bishop with belief that Communion gives Christ's flesh.
facts: His life dates are approximate. He probably died around AD 110.
Clement, Ignatius, and Polycarp belong to the Apostolic Fathers.
His letters distinguish bishops, elders, and deacons.
He linked baptism and Eucharist with the bishop's oversight.

nodes.name: Rise of bishops
nodes.summary: Leadership increasingly centered on one bishop in each city, assisted by elders and deacons. This pattern spread unevenly across Christian communities.
nodes.why: The spread of bishops shaped ordination and claims of apostolic succession. Christians still disagree about whether this leadership is required.
facts: Ignatius describes one bishop with elders and deacons in several Asian churches.
The Didache instructs communities to appoint bishops and deacons.
Early terminology for bishops and elders overlaps.
nodes.disputed: Catholic and Orthodox churches trace bishops to the apostles. Many Protestants distinguish later rule by bishops from New Testament leadership.

nodes.name: Gnostic movements
nodes.summary: Several movements offered salvation through special knowledge and distinguished the highest God from the material world's creator. Church teachers opposed their accounts of Christ.
nodes.why: Gnostic teachings prompted church teachers to defend creation's goodness, Christ's real humanity, and teaching open to everyone.
facts: Gnosticism names diverse schools, rather than one church.
Valentinus taught in the second century.
Irenaeus argued against Gnostic teachings.
These dates approximate the rise and decline of ancient Christian Gnostic schools.
nodes.disputed: Scholars debate which groups count as Gnostic. This node covers ancient Christian Gnostic schools, rather than every religion emphasizing spiritual knowledge.

nodes.name: Marcion's challenge
nodes.summary: Marcion rejected the Old Testament and distinguished its creator God from Jesus' Father. His followers used an edited Luke and ten Pauline letters.
nodes.why: Marcion's rejection of Jewish Scripture prompted churches to defend the Old Testament and clarify which writings belonged in the Bible.
facts: Rome expelled Marcion around AD 144.
His teaching challenged continuity between Israel's Scriptures and Jesus.
Marcionite churches persisted for centuries.
The end date roughly marks their decline in late antiquity.

nodes.name: Montanism
nodes.summary: Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla proclaimed new prophecy in Phrygia. Their movement emphasized the Spirit, strict discipline, and expectation of Christ's return.
nodes.why: The dispute raised questions Christians still face about prophecy, spiritual gifts, church authority, and predictions of the end times.
facts: The movement began during the second century. Its exact starting year is disputed.
Tertullian supported the New Prophecy.
Church leaders challenged its prophetic claims and discipline.
The end date is approximate. Communities survived into later centuries.

nodes.name: New Testament canon
nodes.summary: Churches gradually recognized authoritative apostolic writings. Athanasius listed the familiar 27 New Testament books in 367. Later regional councils endorsed similar lists.
nodes.why: Churches gradually recognized the New Testament books. No single council invented the Bible.
facts: Gospels and Paul's letters circulated before complete book lists.
Athanasius' AD 367 letter lists the familiar 27 New Testament books.
Hippo in 393 and Carthage in 397 endorsed regional canonical lists.
Some eastern churches continued debating particular books after 397.
nodes.disputed: Churches continued recognizing biblical books beyond this date. Christian traditions still differ over the Old Testament and some other books.

nodes.name: Constantine and Milan
nodes.summary: Constantine and Licinius agreed to religious toleration and restoration of Christian property. Constantine's patronage brought churches into a new relationship with imperial power.
nodes.why: Legal protection and imperial support let Christians build public churches. Emperors also began convening councils to settle church disputes.
facts: The agreement protected Christian worship alongside other religions.
It required restoration of confiscated church property.
Constantine later convened Nicaea in 325.
Christianity became the official imperial faith later, under Theodosius.

nodes.name: Arian controversy
nodes.summary: Arius taught that the Son was created and did not share the Father's eternal divine being. Related teachings gained bishops, emperors, and Germanic converts.
nodes.why: The Nicene Creed insists that Jesus is fully divine because Arius taught that the Son was God's highest creature.
facts: Arius taught in Alexandria.
Nicaea condemned his teaching in 325.
The controversy continued long after Nicaea.
Related movements faded in Germanic kingdoms by roughly the seventh century.
nodes.disputed: Arianism groups several differing anti-Nicene positions. Their followers did not all teach precisely what Arius taught.

nodes.name: First Council of Nicaea
nodes.summary: Constantine assembled bishops who rejected Arius and adopted the original Nicene Creed. They affirmed the Son shares the Father's divine being.
nodes.why: Catholics, Orthodox Christians, and most Protestants share Nicaea's confession that Jesus is fully divine.
facts: The creed calls the Son begotten, rather than created.
Homoousios means the Son shares the Father's divine essence.
Nicaea also addressed Easter and church discipline.
The council did not select the books of the Bible.

nodes.name: Augustine of Hippo
nodes.summary: Augustine, bishop of Hippo in North Africa, wrote about grace, sin, Scripture, and the church. His debates shaped Western teaching about baptism and sacraments.
nodes.why: Augustine's teaching still shapes Catholic and Protestant debates about grace, original sin, and whether a minister's failings invalidate baptism.
facts: He lived from AD 354 to 430.
He wrote Confessions and The City of God.
Against Donatists, he defended Christ's authority behind baptism despite a minister's failings.
Against Pelagius, he stressed dependence on God's grace.
nodes.disputed: Catholics and Protestants draw different conclusions from Augustine. Eastern traditions receive his theology with different emphases.

nodes.name: Edict of Thessalonica
nodes.summary: Theodosius I, with Gratian and Valentinian II, declared Nicene Christianity the empire's official faith. Imperial law increasingly disadvantaged rival Christian teachings.
nodes.why: Official status gave Nicene churches public power. Emperors increasingly used law to enforce religious decisions.
facts: The Edict of Thessalonica dates to February 27, 380.
It identifies the faith associated with bishops of Rome and Alexandria.
Later laws restricted pagan worship further.

nodes.name: First Council of Constantinople
nodes.summary: Theodosius convened bishops who reaffirmed Nicene faith and the Holy Spirit's divinity. Tradition links the council to the expanded Nicene Creed.
nodes.why: Its creed still guides worship and teaching about the Trinity. It joins baptism with forgiveness and the hope of resurrection.
facts: The council rejected teachings that denied the Holy Spirit's full divinity.
The creed confesses one baptism for forgiveness of sins.
Chalcedon's records in 451 explicitly attribute the expanded creed to 381.
Bishops ranked Constantinople after Rome because it was New Rome.
nodes.disputed: Scholars debate how the expanded creed was drafted. Chalcedon's surviving records explicitly attribute it to this council.

nodes.name: Council of Ephesus
nodes.summary: Cyril and his supporters condemned Nestorius and affirmed Mary as Theotokos, meaning God-bearer. The title defended Jesus' identity as the incarnate divine Son.
nodes.why: Calling Mary Mother of God affirms that Jesus is one divine person. Disagreement over this teaching divided eastern Christians.
facts: Nestorius objected to unqualified use of Theotokos.
The council affirmed one Christ, rather than two separately acting subjects.
Theotokos does not mean Mary originated God's divine nature.
Rival episcopal assemblies and imperial politics complicated the proceedings.
nodes.disputed: The Church of the East disputes traditional accounts of Nestorius' teaching. Later dialogue recognizes shared belief in Christ's divinity and humanity.

nodes.name: Church of East separation
nodes.summary: Persian churches increasingly separated from Roman imperial churches. Rejection of Ephesus and later reception of Antiochene teaching deepened a division already shaped by politics.
nodes.why: The Church of the East developed outside the Roman Empire. Its separation involved both political independence and disagreements about Christ.
facts: Persian bishops asserted independence from western appeals in 424.
Ephesus in 431 became a marker of doctrinal separation.
Later fifth-century synods consolidated distinctive Christological teaching.
The 431 branch point simplifies a gradual separation.
nodes.disputed: Nestorius did not found this church. Its Persian institutions predated Ephesus, and it rejects the label Nestorian.

nodes.name: Church of the East
nodes.summary: This ancient Persian Christian tradition uses East Syriac worship and accepts the first two ecumenical councils. The Assyrian and Ancient churches continue its independent lineage.
nodes.why: This ancient tradition carried Christian missions across Asia. Its baptism and Eucharist belong to a history beyond the Roman Empire.
facts: Its church institutions existed before the AD 431 map branch.
It confesses one Christ, fully divine and fully human.
Assyrian and Ancient churches continue today. Chaldean Catholics form a separate branch united with Rome.
The Addai and Mari Eucharistic prayer preserves very ancient worship.
nodes.sacraments: Seven mysteries, including Holy Leaven. Baptism grants new birth and includes infants. Eucharist gives Christ's body and blood.
nodes.today: About 400,000 Assyrian members in Iraq, Iran, India, and worldwide diaspora.
nodes.disputed: The estimate covers only the Assyrian church. It rejects the label Nestorian and affirms the Nicene faith.

nodes.name: Five patriarchal sees
nodes.summary: Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem gained regional authority. Councils shaped their standing. The formal system of five patriarchates developed further in the sixth century.
nodes.why: These five cities became centers of church authority. Their roles still shape Catholic and Orthodox disagreements about leadership.
facts: Nicaea recognized Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch's established regional privileges.
Constantinople gained second rank at the council of 381.
Chalcedon recognized Jerusalem's independent regional jurisdiction in 451.
Justinian later gave the five-see system formal imperial expression.
nodes.disputed: Rome rejected Chalcedon's decision to raise Constantinople's rank. Catholics and Orthodox Christians disagree about Rome's authority and the five patriarchates.

nodes.name: Council of Chalcedon
nodes.summary: Bishops affirmed Jesus as one person in two natures, fully divine and fully human. They accepted Leo's Tome and deposed Alexandria's bishop Dioscorus.
nodes.why: Catholics, Eastern Orthodox Christians, and most Protestants accept its teaching about Christ. Oriental Orthodox churches reject its wording.
facts: Emperor Marcian convened the council.
Its definition preserves Christ's divine and human natures without confusion or separation.
The council reaffirmed the creeds associated with 325 and 381.
Many Christians in Egypt and Syria rejected the council.
nodes.disputed: Oriental Orthodox churches reject Chalcedon's wording while affirming Christ's full divinity and humanity. Both sides claim continuity with Cyril of Alexandria.

nodes.name: Chalcedonian separation
nodes.summary: Acceptance or rejection of Chalcedon gradually divided churches into Chalcedonian and non-Chalcedonian communions. Separate hierarchies developed over subsequent generations.
nodes.why: This division separates Oriental Orthodox from Eastern Orthodox churches. Catholics and Eastern Orthodox Christians share the history of accepting Chalcedon.
facts: AD 451 marks the council. Separate church institutions developed gradually afterward.
Egyptian and Syrian opposition helped form lasting churches that rejected Chalcedon.
Armenian rejection developed later.
Modern dialogues have found substantial agreement about Christ's divinity and humanity.
nodes.disputed: Each side saw itself preserving apostolic faith. Politics, language, coercion, and theology all contributed to the gradual separation.

nodes.name: Oriental Orthodox
nodes.summary: Six ancient church traditions reject Chalcedon and follow Cyril's teaching on Christ's united divinity and humanity. They share sacramental worship and communion with one another.
nodes.why: Oriental Orthodox churches preserve ancient baptism and Eucharistic worship. They form a separate family from Eastern Orthodox churches.
facts: The family includes Coptic, Armenian, Syriac, Ethiopian, Eritrean, and Malankara churches.
They accept Nicaea, Constantinople I, and Ephesus.
Miaphysite teaching affirms Christ's full humanity and divinity in one united incarnate nature.
Their apostolic origins predate the AD 451 map branch.
nodes.sacraments: Generally seven holy mysteries. Baptism, usually infant immersion, gives new birth. Chrismation follows. Eucharist truly gives Christ's body and blood, including to baptized infants.
nodes.today: About 60 million in Ethiopia, Egypt, Eritrea, Armenia, Syria, India, diaspora.
nodes.disputed: They reject Eutyches' teaching that Christ's divinity absorbed his humanity. They reject Monophysite as a label for their own teaching.

nodes.name: Chalcedonian church
nodes.summary: Churches accepting Chalcedon confessed one Christ in two natures. Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches inherit this tradition, whose unity faced repeated disputes.
nodes.why: Catholic and Eastern Orthodox baptism and Eucharistic worship grew from a shared history before their medieval separation.
facts: They accept Christ as one person in two complete natures.
Rome and Constantinople remained major centers alongside the other patriarchal sees.
East and West developed different liturgies and approaches to authority.
The AD 1054 endpoint marks a gradual medieval separation.
nodes.sacraments: No universally fixed count. Baptism gives new birth. Eucharist gives Christ's body and blood. Confirmation, penance, ordination, marriage, and anointing develop. Seven becomes standard later.
nodes.today: Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches continue this inheritance. No separate membership.
nodes.disputed: Catholic and Orthodox churches each claim continuity with these churches. Neither describes itself as a new church founded in 1054.
